title: One language, many faces
title_target: Gapo khabar? Hang nak pi mana?
goal: Recognize the varieties of Malay beyond the Kuala Lumpur standard — the Malaysian states, Brunei and Singapore — so you don't panic when you hear a sentence where you don't know a single word.
bekal: recognizing the main features of the Kelantan, Kedah, Sarawak, Sabah and Negeri Sembilan dialects
knowing how Malay differs in Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore
having rescue phrases for when you really don't catch anything

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Three people, three states
dialogs.intro: Friday night in the college kitchen. Aina (from Kelantan), Haziq (from Kedah) and Sarah are cooking together. Sarah has just realized that her two friends sound completely different when they phone their families.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Aina, tadi awak cakap dengan mak awak — saya tak faham langsung!
lines.id: Aina, just now you were talking to your mum — I didn't understand a thing!
lines.literal: Aina, earlier you speak with mother your — I not understand at-all!

lines.speaker: Aina:
lines.text: Hahaha! Tu loghat Kelantan. Kami cakap 'Gapo khabar?' bukan 'Apa khabar?'
lines.id: Hahaha! That's the Kelantan dialect. We say 'Gapo khabar?', not 'Apa khabar?'
lines.literal: hahaha! that dialect Kelantan. we say 'gapo khabar?' not 'apa khabar?'

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: Gapo? It's like a different language altogether.

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Kelantan memang paling jauh. Orang KL pun tak faham.
lines.id: Kelantan really is the furthest from standard. Even people from KL don't understand it.
lines.literal: Kelantan indeed most far. people KL even not understand.

lines.speaker: Aina:
lines.text: Haziq pun sama je. Dia orang Kedah — 'hang', 'depa', 'pi'.
lines.id: Haziq's no different. He's from Kedah — 'hang', 'depa', 'pi'.
lines.literal: Haziq also same just. he person Kedah — 'hang', 'depa', 'pi'.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Jadi 'Hang nak pi mana?' tu 'Awak nak pergi mana?'
lines.id: So 'Hang nak pi mana?' is 'Where are you going?'
lines.literal: so 'hang nak pi mana?' that 'you want go where?'

lines.speaker: Aina:
lines.text: Tapi kat kelas, kat TV, kat pejabat — semua orang cakap baku. Jangan risau.
lines.id: But in class, on TV, at the office — everyone speaks standard Malay. Don't worry.
lines.literal: but at class, at TV, at office — all people speak standard. don't worry.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Nasib baik. Kalau semua cakap Kelantan, habislah saya.
lines.id: Thank goodness. If everyone spoke Kelantanese, I'd be finished.
lines.literal: luck good. if all speak Kelantan, finished-lah I.

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Takpe. Kalau tak faham, cakap je: 'Boleh cakap slow sikit?' Semua orang faham.
lines.id: No problem. If you don't understand, just say: 'Could you speak a bit slower?' Everyone understands that.
lines.literal: not-matter. if not understand, say just: 'can speak slow little?' all people understand.

notes: **Loghat** = dialect, accent (spelled with *gh*). Related words: *dialek* (dialect), *pelat* (accent — unit 1). Malaysians talk about *loghat negeri* (state dialects).

**Langsung** at the end of a negative sentence means **at all**. *Tak faham langsung* = "didn't understand at all". This use of *langsung* is typically Malaysian (its basic meaning is "direct, straight").
**Tangkap** = to catch, also in the sense of "catch on, get it". *Cepat awak tangkap* = you catch on fast.

**Slow** — and here's a fact to accept: English words turn up everywhere in Malaysian conversation, even when the Malay word exists (*perlahan*). It isn't a sign of a broken language; it's a feature of a multilingual society.
**Baku** = standard. *Bahasa Melayu baku* = Standard Malay, taught in schools and used in the media. That's what you're learning in this module.

grammars.title: The five state dialects you'll hear most
body: You **don't need** to master any of these dialects. What you need is to recognize that what you're hearing is a dialect — not a sign that your Malay has failed. This table is built so you can guess where someone is from with just a few words.

head: Dialect
Main features
Example
Standard
rows: final *a* → *o*, many words of its own
Gapo khabar? Demo nok gi mano?
Apa khabar? Awak nak pergi mana?
Hang nak pi mana? Depa dah balik.
Awak nak pergi mana? Mereka dah balik.
Den nak poi. Ekau nak apo?
Saya nak pergi. Awak nak apa?
Kamek sik tauk. Kitak dari sitok?
Saya tak tahu. Awak dari sini?
this is the basis of the standard

after: **Kelantanese is the furthest from the standard.** It's not just the accent: the vocabulary differs (*gapo* for what, *demo* for you, *kawe* for I, *nok* for want, *gi* for go), and even people from Kuala Lumpur often need time to adjust. If you go to Kota Bharu and catch nothing, that's normal — even for Malaysians.

**Kedah is easier.** You only need to swap three words: *hang* (you), *depa* (they), *pi* (go). The rest is close to standard, just sharper-sounding, and a final *a* stays a full *a* (where KL Malay softens it to a weak *uh* sound).

blocks.text: Malay is an official language in **Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore**. All three use the same spelling and an almost identical standard — but each feels different.

head: Malaysia
Brunei
Singapore
rows: national language (English is the working language)

blocks.text: **Brunei** uses standard Malay almost identical to Malaysia's in writing and broadcasting, but everyday **Brunei Malay** is quite different — partly because its vowel system is simpler, so *orang* sounds like *urang* and *besar* like *basar*. Brunei also keeps a very rich palace vocabulary, being the only Malay sultanate where the sultan still rules in full.

**Singapore** made Malay its **national language** — the national anthem, *Majulah Singapura*, is in Malay, and so are military parade commands. But the everyday working language is English, so Singapore Malay is spoken mainly by the Malay community and mixes in more English.

blocks.title: And what about Indonesian?
items: Indonesian and Malaysian Malay are **two standard varieties of one language** — much like British and American English, or European and Brazilian Portuguese.

Their spelling has been **unified since 1972** through the Joint Rumi Spelling (Ejaan Rumi Bersama / Ejaan Yang Disempurnakan). Before that, Malaysia wrote *chair* for *cair* (liquid) and Indonesia wrote *tjair*.
The **Brunei–Indonesia–Malaysia Language Council (MABBIM)** still meets today to align new terminology.
What has **not** been aligned is everyday vocabulary — which is why Malaysian Malay and Indonesian can feel so different in daily life.

⚠️ Never call Malay "a dialect of Indonesian" or vice versa in front of speakers of either. Both are sovereign standard languages, and the history runs the opposite way from what many assume: Indonesian was standardized **from** Malay.

sections.title: When you really don't catch anything

blocks.text: It will happen, and there's nothing wrong with that. Keep these phrases handy:

head: Malay
English
rows: Could you speak a bit slower?
I'm Indonesian, I've only just started learning.
Your accent is lovely to listen to.

blocks.text: That last sentence isn't empty flattery — it works. Malaysians are generally proud of their state dialect, and showing interest in someone's *loghat* almost always opens a warmer conversation than asking them to speak standard Malay.

blocks.title: How to train your ear
items: **Start with the news.** Buletin Utama TV3, Berita RTM, Astro Awani — all standard Malay, clear, at a moderate pace.
**Then Kuala Lumpur dramas.** Everyday Selangor/KL speech, the closest to the standard.
**Then Malaysian podcasts and YouTube.** That's where the street Malay of unit 12 lives.
**State dialects last**, and only if you live in that state. There's no point learning Kelantanese if you work in Cyberjaya.
⚠️ **Don't start with songs.** Malay lyrics are full of poetic words and inverted word order that nobody uses in conversation.
